name: North Korea
headline: North Korean law gives patients no right to their records and no say over sharing, while the UN finds state surveillance growing.

access.summary: No law we read gives a patient the right to see or copy their medical record. The Medical Law says a diagnosis is told to the patient, but a diagnosis judged harmful to treatment may be told only to the guardian.
detail: The Medical Law (1997, last amended in the text we read on 20 November 2012) requires hospitals to write case histories, diagnosis certificates and prescriptions accurately and to keep originals or copies for a set period (Article 32). It gives the patient no right to see or copy them.
Article 20 says a confirmed diagnosis is told to the patient, but a diagnosis that could harm treatment may be told only to the guardian.
A citizen may petition for a medical appraisal and must be told the result; an appraisal document may be issued 'if necessary' (Articles 36 and 41).
There is no patient portal. Whether laws newer than the 2012 texts add any access right is not verified.

sources.title: Medical Law of the DPRK, 2012 text (Unification Law Database, Ministry of Government Legislation, Seoul)
Public Health Law of the DPRK, 2012 text (Unification Law Database, Ministry of Government Legislation, Seoul)

control.summary: Patients must consent to surgery and to the use of organs, but the Medical Law makes hospitals register every patient found in check-ups and report them to the 'relevant bodies'. We found no choice over sharing and no access log.
detail: Medical Law Article 26 requires the patient's consent before surgery, or the guardian's if the patient is unconscious. Article 27 requires consent to use organs or tissue from a living, brain-dead or dead person.
Article 15 requires hospitals to register patients found in medical check-ups and notify the relevant bodies, which must act on the results.
Article 40 allows an autopsy of a hospital death without the guardian's consent.
No rule lets a person limit who sees their health data, opt out of sharing or see who accessed it.

privacy.summary: We found no data protection law, no regulator and no medical secrecy duty in the health laws we read. A UN report in 2025 found general surveillance 'more pervasive, aided by advances in technology'.
detail: Neither the Medical Law nor the Public Health Law sets a duty of confidentiality, breach rules or penalties for misuse of patient data. Both make officials liable only for 'serious consequences' to health work.
The UN High Commissioner's 2025 report says state control over citizens' lives was 'the most absolute in decades' and that surveillance technology helped increase it.
The 2023 State Secrets Protection Law, as summarised by Seoul's legislation ministry, defines secrets as anything tied to state security and interests.
North Korea has no EU adequacy decision, so EU health data sent there would need GDPR transfer safeguards.

commercial.summary: No law limits selling health data or using it for marketing; the health laws we read say nothing on sale or reuse of records. Care is moving to fees and a 'health insurance fund', which analysts link to the free-care clause dropped from the 2026 constitution.
detail: The Public Health Law (2012) still promises free medicines, diagnosis, tests and hospital stays (Article 10), but neither it nor the Medical Law mentions sale, transfer or reuse of patient data.
The UN reported in 2025 that access to care depends on ability to pay and that patients must bring their own drugs and supplies.
The 2026 constitution dropped the 'universal free medical care' clause, and Kim Jong Un's March 2026 speech called for expanding care financed by a health insurance fund (KINU).
A Chinese business visitor told News1 that patients at Pyongyang General Hospital queue to pay per service. How insurance data is used is not verified.

journey.summary: The health ministry reported a telemedicine network linking Pyongyang with hospitals in 12 provinces and 215 county hospitals, but its own plan describes unintegrated health information systems. No shared patient record exists.
detail: The Ministry of Public Health's 2016 to 2020 strategic plan says the telemedicine system connected Pyongyang and provincial hospitals in 12 provinces and 215 city, district and county hospitals.
The same plan names 'sectoral (unintegrated) health information systems' as a gap, with lower levels reduced to data collection only.
In February 2026 WHO ran a webinar with the ministry on electronic health records, FHIR and a phased national digital health roadmap. No roadmap has been published that we found.
A Rodong Sinmun plan for one digital network from central hospitals to homes is described by analysts (not verified in the original).

clinical.summary: A doctor in a county hospital can consult specialists in Pyongyang by video link, but no system lets a treating clinician see a patient's record from other providers. Records stay as paper or local files.
detail: The Medical Law tells hospitals to refer hard-to-diagnose cases to a doctors' council or a specialist hospital (Article 16).
The telemedicine network links central and county hospitals for consultation. An October 2025 state media video showed it used mainly to train rural staff, per NK Economy.
We found no shared electronic record, emergency access rule or record transfer rule between providers.

research.summary: No rule on research consent, opt-out or reuse of patient data was found, so this sits at the no-consent base of 40. No safeguard counts: the Medical Law's approval of new diagnostic methods and council review of gene therapy are clinical, not research, controls.
detail: Public Health Law Articles 29 to 33 tell state research institutes to put treatment and prevention problems first and to work on Koryo (traditional) medicine and new drugs and devices. They say nothing on participant consent.
Medical Law Article 18 requires approval from the 'relevant body' for a newly created or introduced diagnostic method. Article 27 requires council review for gene therapy and transplants.
No research ethics committee, opt-out or register of data uses was verified.

ai.summary: We found no rules for AI in clinical care: no AI law, no health AI guidance and no regulation of medical software. A February 2026 WHO webinar only introduced AI governance to ministry staff.
detail: WHO's 2026 webinar with the Ministry of Public Health covered generative AI for clinical decision support, and 'the importance of ethical safeguards, data protection, national ownership and governance frameworks'.
Kim Il Sung University researchers have published deep learning work on chest X-ray images using a US NIH dataset, per NK Economy.
No device rules for AI, change control or human oversight duty were found.

journeyNote: Hospitals link to Pyongyang by video for consultation and training, and disease reports flow to the state. No shared patient record links clinics, labs, pharmacies or the new insurance fund.

laws.name: Medical Law
laws.what: Records must be kept; diagnosis may be told only to guardian; patients registered and reported to authorities.

laws.name: Public Health Law
laws.what: Promises free care and section doctors; state leads medical research; no data or confidentiality rules.

laws.name: Socialist Constitution, Article 49
laws.what: Revised health clause drops universal free care, section doctors and preventive medicine wording.

laws.name: State Secrets Protection Law
laws.what: Defines state secrets broadly as anything tied to state security and interests, with criminal penalties.

news.headline: Analysis says North Korea now charges fees and runs a health insurance fund
news.why: Care, and data about it, now depends on payment and workplace enrolment.

news.headline: New North Korean constitution deletes the free medical care clause
news.why: Removes the main constitutional promise patients could point to.

news.headline: Analyst warns state digital health plan could turn health data into surveillance
news.why: A national network with no privacy law puts health records in state hands.

news.headline: WHO trains health ministry staff on digital records, FHIR and AI
news.why: First step toward a national digital health roadmap and data governance.
